In the previous session, due to network issues, I couldn’t send this message in time. I’d like to ask about the representation of drawings at different stages, especially the IFC stage and construction drawing stage. Could you share some examples of drawings with relatively lighter detailing and depth?

In our CBD project, we encountered inconsistencies in the requirements from the supervision teams. The project consists of 20 buildings, divided into 10 construction departments, each corresponding to a different supervision team. Some supervisors had higher demands for drawings—for example, in slab-lowering plans, they required detailed annotations for HVAC material specifications, references to approval documents, and even minutiae like connectors for distribution boxes, bolts, and nuts. While these requests aren’t unreasonable, they might be overly meticulous.
Regarding the issue of low volume you mentioned, can you hear me clearly now?

Alright, let’s begin today’s lecture. The main topic is the design of power distribution systems. I believe everyone here has some basic understanding of this subject, so I’ll proceed at a relatively fast pace. The design of power distribution systems primarily includes the following aspects:

It is necessary to draw a Single Line Diagram. Prior to this, Load Calculation should be performed, and after completing the load classification, the calculation can be finalized to generate the single line diagram.

When drawing the single line diagram, the selection of the Voltage System must be determined, including the voltage level and applicable category. In North America, the selection of voltage systems is relatively complex, whereas in China, the 220V/380V system is simpler. For large industrial systems, such as those involving large motors, a low-voltage power supply system cannot be used.

Additionally, coordination with the local power department is required to ensure the rationality of the incoming line setup. The Emergency Power system is a fundamental requirement of building codes, while UPS systems are typically used for critical loads such as IT communication equipment, building automation systems, and security access control systems.

After completing the load calculation and single line diagram design, the location and scale of the Electrical Room, substation, or generator room must be determined, and coordination with relevant disciplines such as architecture, structure, and HVAC is necessary.

Regarding Power Quality, awareness in China is currently insufficient, and related standards are not yet comprehensive. In contrast, North America has stricter standards and requirements, including various technical indicators for power supply quality. At the same time, the coordination of protective devices must also be considered.

Additionally, the selection of major electrical equipment is also a critical aspect. During the distribution system design process, commonly used tools include drawing and calculation software. Simultaneously, coordination with other disciplines is required.

The single-line diagram holds an extremely important position in the design.

As you may have understood, in a project, completing the Single Line Diagram actually accounts for 30% to 40% of the total workload, with the remaining tasks simply following the diagram’s execution. So, what does a Single Line Diagram typically include? I will explain in detail later, covering aspects like technical levels involved.

The Single Line Diagram is closely related to power system design calculations. The diagram includes critical annotations such as equipment capacity, short-circuit current capacity, motor starting issues, harmonic problems, and arc flash hazards—all of which have detailed technical specifications in North America.

The Single Line Diagram and Power Study are complementary and require continuous updates at different design stages. This is because Power Study calculations first require model creation, and this modeling process is based on the Single Line Diagram. In North America, specific Feeder Schedules are used for different distribution panels and loads to guide details like large-conductor selection and conduit routing.

Additionally, the Single Line Diagram often needs to reflect the grounding system’s single-line representation, i.e., grounding theory. If time permits, a typical Single Line Diagram will be analyzed, though today’s schedule might be tight.

Regarding load calculation and its classification, loads are mainly divided into two major categories, but there are finer subdivisions within emergency loads. When performing load calculations, whether for normal or emergency loads, the total load must be considered when selecting the incoming line capacity. However, when choosing a generator, only the emergency load needs to be considered. Emergency loads are typically categorized into three types: fire protection loads, life safety loads (such as emergency lighting, fire alarm systems, smoke control systems, etc.), and critical loads (such as loads in hospitals that could lead to property damage or casualties).

In load calculations, redundancy configurations such as one-duty-one-standby or two-duty-one-standby must be considered, where only the capacity of simultaneously operating loads needs to be calculated. Additionally, seasonal loads such as summer cooling and winter heating require comparing the magnitudes of the two and selecting the larger load for calculation.

Different countries, regions, and industrial sectors have varying classifications and definitions for loads. For example, in the construction industry, load classification and calculation methods differ between North America, mainland China, and the former Soviet Union. In North America, load classification is determined by building codes, while load calculations are governed by electrical codes.

In some cases, owners may have special requirements for emergency loads. Even if certain loads do not fall under fire protection, life safety, or critical loads, they may still need to be connected to the generator bus. These factors must also be taken into account during load calculations.

Definitions and calculation methods for load vary across different countries and industries.

For instance, in North America, “Connected Load” refers to the total power rating of all electrical equipment, but this value cannot be directly used in design, as it would result in an oversized system. Another concept is “Demand Load”, which represents the actual maximum load required, taking into account the simultaneous use of equipment. Meanwhile, “Design Load” is typically larger than “Demand Load,” incorporating safety margins and various coefficients.

The National Electrical Code (NEC) provides detailed explanations of these concepts.

When calculating demand load, the diversity factor must be considered. Different building types have distinct load characteristic coefficients, and redundancy configurations such as "one in operation with one standby" schemes should also be accounted for. Load sources include not only electrical equipment like lighting and sockets but also requirements from other disciplines, such as elevator parameters submitted by mechanical engineers and special requirements from the client. Additionally, various on-site electrical loads must be factored in.

Different types of loads exhibit unique characteristics. For example, elevators have steady-state loads during normal operation but generate instantaneous impact loads during motor startup. Equipment such as air handling units (AHUs), chillers, cooling towers (CTs), circulating pumps, fans, boilers, electric heaters, and welding machines all have distinct load profiles. In electrical distribution system design, specific considerations must be made based on load categories, with these parameters typically provided by design codes or equipment manufacturers.

Load calculation methods vary by project phase. During the preliminary conceptual design stage, due to limited detailed information, the unit area index method is commonly used for reasonable estimation. In the schematic design phase, relatively conservative estimates are recommended to allow flexibility for adjustments during detailed design.

The voltage system in North America is more complex than in mainland China or Egypt. To briefly explain, this may not be highly relevant to some listeners. High-voltage systems typically refer to 110 kV and above, with 500 kV classified as extra-high voltage. Those with a power system automation background may be familiar with grid-related courses, while electrical automation professionals generally have less exposure. Currently, our focus is primarily on medium-voltage and lower systems.

In North America, medium-voltage systems encompass multiple voltage levels ranging from 4,000 volts, 13.8 kV, 25 kV, 46.4 kV, up to 69 kV. Low-voltage systems are equally complex: Canada uses 600V/347V, while the U.S. employs 480V/277V, equivalent to China’s 220V/380V. Additionally, there is a unique 208V/120V voltage level widely used in Canadian residential and office buildings. The 120V/208V corresponds to China’s 220V/380V, whereas 600V/347V and 480V/277V belong to a higher-tier voltage system.

North American residential systems primarily use a 120V/240V dual live-wire voltage system, which is neither three-phase nor purely single-phase, marking a significant difference from Chinese systems. Control equipment often operates on 24V AC/DC power, while devices like computers use 5V DC power.

Three-phase three-wire grounded system (Delta connection), suitable for balanced three-phase loads like motors.  
Three-phase four-wire plus ground system (Wye connection), capable of supplying both three-phase and single-phase loads.  

Voltage drop from the supply point to the load end must not exceed 5%. Power system calculation tools (Power Study) can automatically determine voltage drop parameters, considering factors like conductor size, distance, and load. If voltage drop exceeds limits, solutions include:  
1. Increasing conductor cross-sectional area to reduce impedance.  
2. Adjusting transformer tap settings to raise supply voltage by approximately 2.5%.  
3. Installing voltage regulation equipment (Power Conditioner) at the load end.  

Special attention is required for voltage disturbances:  
1. Sudden voltage spikes caused by lightning strikes.  
2. Voltage sags or surges.  
3. Voltage rise due to third-harmonic distortion.

Special attention is required for voltage disturbances: 1. Sudden voltage spikes caused by lightning strikes. 2. Voltage sags or surges. 3. Voltage rise due to third-harmonic distortion.

In North American office designs, neutral conductors are typically sized at double capacity. When three-phase imbalance currents are significant, neutral current can reach 1.7 times the load current. For lightning-induced voltage disturbances, TVSS (Transient Voltage Surge Suppressors) or SPD (Surge Protective Devices) are commonly installed for protection.

Regarding the fundamental concepts of voltage, high voltage and low voltage exhibit distinct characteristics in power systems. High-voltage transmission enables large-capacity power delivery while maintaining better voltage drop performance. For the same load, high-voltage transmission results in lower current, which means conductor cross-sections can be reduced, thereby saving costs.

However, due to higher insulation requirements, the cost of high-voltage equipment increases accordingly. In industrial applications, large electrical equipment typically operates at various high-voltage levels. Additionally, transient processes during motor startup may cause significant voltage dips.

When high-voltage power supply is adopted, voltage drops are more likely to meet regulatory requirements; whereas low-voltage power supply may lead to sudden voltage drops, preventing motors from starting normally or completing state transitions.

Thus, a 200% neutral current. As mentioned earlier, the main issue currently stems from some non-linear loads, such as UPSs, VMDs, and electronic devices like computers, which generate harmonics, leading to excessively high neutral current levels. Next, I will discuss the issues related to the incoming line section.

The incoming line section primarily requires coordination with the local power utility, including the selection of the incoming line location and routing method. The routing methods can include overhead, direct bury, or duct bank. Currently, large-scale buildings mostly adopt the direct bury method rather than overhead.

For different regions and projects, it is necessary to negotiate with the utility company to determine whether the substation will be constructed by the utility company or the client. This involves aspects such as the design cycle, scope, and final project cost. Substations can be categorized into indoor and outdoor types, and the design scheme should be determined based on the specific project.

Coordination with the local power utility also requires attention to differences in peak and off-peak electricity pricing among different utility companies. Additionally, during the design process, power system analysis calculations, including short-circuit current calculations, must be performed, which require an understanding of the system capacity. Coordination is also needed for metering requirements and protection relay integration.

Different power utilities have specific requirements for power factor and harmonics. For example, the power factor is typically required to be above 0.9. Harmonic-related requirements will be detailed in the power quality section.

Next, I will introduce the Emergency Power Supply System (EPSS). The design of the emergency power supply system will be covered in detail in the next lecture. The generator is the core component of the EPSS, and its types include diesel generators, natural gas generators, and dual-fuel (diesel-natural gas) generators. Installation methods can be categorized as indoor or outdoor.

Capacity selection for generators is critical. Typically, we can perform the calculations ourselves or rely on generator manufacturers (such as Caterpillar and Cummins) to assist using specialized software. The calculations are based on single-line diagrams and load conditions. Although all loads are emergency loads, different load stages (e.g., starting phase, running phase) will influence the final generator selection.

Relevant standards were mentioned in the first lecture. Canada adopts the CSA C282 and NFPA 110 standards, which specify requirements for generators. The operation mode of generators depends on system design and project needs. For example, small-scale projects may use a single standalone generator (Standalone mode), while large-scale projects may require multiple generators operating in parallel.

The emergency power supply system must be equipped with an Automatic Transfer Switch (ATS). ATS units are divided into three categories: dedicated to fire protection loads, fire protection load priority, and dedicated to other loads. Additionally, the ATS must coordinate with elevator controllers. During the transition between grid power and generator power, if an elevator is in operation, communication and coordination between the two must be ensured.

There is a grounding coordination issue between the generator and the ATS. When selecting an ATS, considerations must be made regarding whether to adopt a three-pole or four-pole configuration, as well as whether to switch the neutral line during the transition between utility power and the generator. This is a common technical challenge, and even many experienced engineers may not fully grasp it. Grounding issues in electrical design are indeed quite complex.

Regarding the switching methods of ATS between utility power and backup power, there are primarily three types:

1. Open Transition: Directly switching from utility power to the generator or vice versa, resulting in a brief power interruption during the transition.

2. Close Transition: Achieving seamless switching between utility power and the generator, with no power interruption perceived by the load.

3. Parallel Operation: The generator and utility power remain essentially synchronized, allowing both to operate simultaneously.

It is important to note that for seamless switching and parallel operation, approval from the local power supply authority is required, as this may impact grid power flow and even cause disturbances.

It is important to note that for seamless switching and parallel operation, approval from the local power supply authority is required, as this may impact grid power flow and even cause disturbances.

In terms of generator control, there is a Load Shedding function. When project budgets are limited, a smaller-capacity generator can be selected, which automatically sheds non-critical loads after emergency power switching. Additionally, generator installation requires coordination with structural engineering: ground installations require a concrete pad, while floor installations necessitate structural reinforcement design.

In cold regions of North America, outdoor-installed generators must be equipped with a Block Heater or Battery Charger. Since generators may remain inactive for extended periods, it is essential to ensure the starting battery remains charged year-round to prevent insufficient battery power from causing startup failure.

In cold regions during winter, generator engine housings must be equipped with electric heaters to ensure normal startup in low-temperature environments—a critical design consideration during the planning phase. Additionally, attention must be paid to load banks and mandatory testing procedures.

The role of a load bank is to simulate real-world loads. Since generators serve as long-term standby equipment for emergency use, prolonged inactivity may lead to startup failures during critical moments. Therefore, regular testing (e.g., biannually or quarterly) via load banks is essential—this involves connecting the generator to simulated loads while maintaining normal grid power to verify its startup performance.

For small-scale projects, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) or battery systems are often used as emergency power sources. For instance, low-rise buildings with emergency lighting or spaces without ventilation requirements can rely solely on battery systems, such as FARWAR or emergency lighting systems (Emergence Lighting).

In recent years, advancements in electric vehicle controls and battery energy storage technologies have enabled high-capacity batteries to potentially replace traditional generators. Notably, the rise of modular smart grid systems—which integrate solar panels, generators, battery storage, and grid power to form small-scale smart grids—represents the future direction of energy systems. The specific applications of UPS will be discussed in subsequent sections.

UPS technology has evolved over many years and was traditionally used primarily in data centers or large control centers. There are various types of UPS systems, including always-charged and non-charged types, depending on their internal wiring configurations. In large-scale projects, centralized large-capacity UPS systems can be adopted to power all electrical loads through a distribution system, or distributed small-capacity UPS systems can be deployed locally to supply power to nearby loads—these are referred to as centralized or localized solutions.

UPS systems are categorized into commercial and industrial applications, analogous to the distinction between civilian and military products. UPS units for different fields must meet specific requirements during manufacturing. A typical UPS system includes AC/DC conversion modules and battery packs, with some products featuring an integrated design while others separate the conversion modules from the batteries.

UPS selection must account for current demand, backup duration (ampere-hours), and instantaneous peak load (measured in kVA or kW). Additionally, technical parameters such as power factor and harmonic distortion coefficient should be considered. While the technical details of the AC/DC conversion section are not elaborated here, it is important to note that battery packs have a limited lifespan. Traditional UPS batteries often experience significant performance degradation after five years, requiring frequent replacements. Although modern batteries have seen extended lifespans due to technological advancements, engineering designs must still factor in long-term replacement costs.

As electronic equipment, UPS systems are sensitive to environmental conditions. In North America, for example, electrical rooms often house heat-generating devices like step-down transformers (e.g., 600V/208V or 480V/208V), leading to high indoor temperatures during summer, which poses challenges for UPS operation.

Therefore, measures such as ventilation or even cooling are required to maintain equipment temperature. For Electroloom, an ambient temperature of 30°C is sufficient, while generators can also operate normally at 30°C. However, UPS systems have stricter requirements, typically needing to be controlled below 25°C.

Regarding the largest UPS configurations in data centers, two key metrics are primarily involved: Tier Rating and Redundancy. Tier Rating is essentially a measure of redundancy levels, generally divided into four tiers, with Tier 4 being the highest standard, featuring a fully redundant (Fully Redundant) design to ensure 100% backup systems for all components.

For environmental requirements, if non-sealed batteries are used (now relatively rare), battery rooms also require exhaust ventilation and environmental control, sometimes even necessitating explosion-proof design considerations. As for UPS sizing, it is primarily determined by parameters such as ampere-hours (Ah) and kVA, selected based on load demands. Typically, UPS systems are essential for facilities like data centers and control centers where electronic equipment cannot tolerate power interruptions.

It is worth noting that large UPS equipment is heavy, requiring structural engineers to account for load-bearing requirements to implement corresponding structural reinforcement designs.

It is worth noting that large UPS equipment is heavy, requiring structural engineers to account for load-bearing requirements to implement corresponding structural reinforcement designs.

Now let’s discuss the key design considerations for electrical rooms or related spaces, including generator rooms and UPS rooms. First, sufficient space must be ensured for installing electrical equipment, while accounting for future replacement, installation transportation, and operational maintenance requirements—specifically the clearance. Specific requirements for different equipment come from two sources: electrical code regulations and manufacturer specifications. For instance, in North America, general electrical equipment typically requires 1 meter of clearance, while drawer-type switchgear may need 1.5 meters.

Electrical rooms should be located close to the load center while meeting environmental requirements such as ventilation and cooling. Additionally, structural conditions must be provided; if the load is substantial, the cooling load for mechanical systems must also be considered. This means the mechanical team must design cooling systems based on the heat output of electrical equipment, necessitating data on equipment quantity and operational heat generation.

In North America, fully sprinklered buildings allow sprinkler heads in electrical rooms because firefighting prioritizes overall suppression, whereas domestic practices require power shutdowns. During normal operation, only sprinkler systems are permitted in electrical rooms—other water pipes should be avoided. Electrical equipment such as high/low-voltage switchgear and distribution panels are typically selected to allow general sprinkler exposure, with no mandatory distance requirements between panels and water sources. However, in residential or office settings, outlets within 1.5 meters of water sources must have protection features.

The fire rating for electrical rooms is usually 1-hour or 2-hour, depending on the building type. Doors, windows, walls, and floor slabs must meet corresponding fire standards as determined by building codes. Additionally, electrical rooms should avoid locations above potential water leakage areas, such as mechanical rooms or water tanks. While these are not mandatory under North American codes, they represent good practice.

This is actually determined by the architect based on building codes. Of course, we architects need you to provide other requirements, such as the size of the door, etc.

Specific requirements regarding area, location, and floor height need to be clarified in advance. Additionally, the routing of various professional pipelines, including conduits and cable trays for electrical systems, as well as air ducts and sprinkler pipes for mechanical systems, must be coordinated to avoid conflicts.

During the design process, detailed enlarged drawings must be provided for Electrical Rooms. Since conventional flow diagrams cannot adequately display the details, special attention should be paid to the following points:

Fire Alarm System Equipment: Smoke detectors, alarm devices, and other fire detection/alarm equipment must be installed in electrical rooms.

Access Control System: Depending on the specific project design requirements and the client’s needs, access control systems may need to be installed in electrical rooms.

Grounding System: Each electrical room should be equipped with a grounding busbar, which must be directly connected to the outdoor grounding system.

Door Dimensions: Sufficient dimensions must be reserved for electrical room door openings. For electrical rooms located on the second floor or higher, hoisting equipment may be required for installation, so corresponding installation openings should be reserved.

The above designs must be coordinated with architectural layout and mechanical disciplines.

For example, when configuring diesel generators, it is necessary to properly plan the layout of fuel pipelines, oil pumps, fuel storage tanks, as well as ventilation and exhaust systems. For UPS rooms, special hazardous environment requirements must also be considered.

It is worth noting that in North America, diesel generators are typically not designed to meet explosion-proof standards, but battery systems may have such requirements. Electrical equipment rooms in ordinary buildings generally do not require special protection, whereas industrial settings (especially petrochemical facilities) commonly impose such demands.

During the design process, it is advisable to position generator rooms or UPS rooms as close as possible to the main distribution room to optimize cable routing efficiency. Such designs involve multiple factors and require a relatively long technical digestion period.

Let’s discuss power quality issues. Power quality involves several fundamental concepts. For instance, when a motor starts, if the voltage drop is too significant, it may cause difficulty in starting. Additionally, the voltage and frequency of electrical equipment are crucial. Frequency has a relatively minor impact, but voltage must be maintained within ±10% of the rated value. Excessive voltage can shorten insulation lifespan, while insufficient voltage may cause equipment overheating or failure to start. Furthermore, harmonics or interference can introduce noise to control systems, affecting normal operation. Severe harmonics can also lead to conductor overheating and even fires.

Key indicators of power quality include voltage level. In North America, the steady-state voltage drop standard is 5%, excluding transient voltage drops during motor startup. Overvoltage can damage equipment such as motors, so surge protective devices (SPDs) are typically installed. Frequency disturbances are less relevant to distribution systems, but grid frequency reflects the balance between generation and load. The allowable frequency deviation in domestic grids ranges from ±0.2Hz to ±0.5Hz. A higher frequency indicates excess generation and insufficient load, while a lower frequency suggests insufficient generation and excessive load.

In power grids, reactive power is related to voltage, while active power is tied to frequency. This is essential for generators and grids to maintain voltage levels. Understanding these basic concepts helps in better grasping related design methodologies.

One indicator requirement for three-phase imbalance is not a mandatory code provision but rather a good engineering practice. As previously mentioned, voltage should not experience sudden spikes or drops, and current must also maintain three-phase balance. The degree of imbalance should not exceed 25%. For transient overvoltages caused by lightning, SPDs (Surge Protective Devices) must be installed.

Harmonics cause distortion in voltage and current waveforms, with a typical requirement not exceeding 5%. The IEEE Color Book series includes a dedicated volume discussing harmonics. Harmonic calculation is also part of power system studies (Power Study). Domestic adoption of related standards may still be limited. Internationally, grid modeling software is commonly used to calculate harmonic distortion based on distribution system models, with filters designed for mitigation according to harmonic orders (e.g., 3rd, 5th, 7th) and magnitudes. Local utilities conduct testing, measurement, and analytical calculations.

In comparison, the first two approaches are more feasible.

This device is used to adjust grid voltage and belongs to power quality improvement equipment, with a relatively high price. It is typically only applied in precision composite equipment that demands extremely high voltage and power quality standards.

In North America, such devices are referred to as power factor correction equipment. Taking residential buildings as an example, high-rise structures require the installation of such devices.

High-rise buildings have a fundamental load calculation method. Taking 100 households as an example, the load calculation for each household is as follows: First, determine a basic load, which is calculated based on the area. Additionally, other loads are included, such as lighting, sockets, appliances, stoves, water heaters, and air conditioning. The basic load plus these additional loads constitutes the total load.

The specific calculation method is: The basic load for the first household is 12 kilowatts, calculated at 100%; the second and third households are calculated at 65%, meaning two households multiplied by 65% of 12 kilowatts; subsequent households are calculated at decreasing rates of 40%, 25%, and 10%. Therefore, as the number of households increases, the load factor gradually decreases. For example, the first 20 households are calculated at different factors, and each household beyond 20 is calculated at 10%. This means the total load for 80 households is not 80 multiplied by 10 kilowatts, but 80 multiplied by 1 kilowatt.

The load calculation for commercial buildings varies depending on the project type, such as office buildings, warehouses, hospitals, and schools, each having different calculation methods. This part falls under the category of electrical planning, which will be discussed in detail later if the opportunity arises.

Next, we will introduce electromechanical protection and its coordination.

Electromechanical protection primarily involves low-voltage and medium-voltage systems. Low-voltage protection devices include fuses, contactors, disconnect breakers, and circuit breakers.

There is a wide variety of electromechanical protection devices, such as over-current relays, overloaded relays, directional relays, distance relays, zero-sequence relays, and time-delay relays. Among these, directional protection, distance protection, and zero-sequence protection are mainly applied in medium- and high-voltage systems, while low-voltage systems primarily rely on over-current, overload, and ground-fault protection.

For transformers and motors, protection in medium- and high-voltage systems is more complex. Protection devices include trip units such as electronic trip units, magnetic trip units, and thermal trip units. Circuit breakers in medium-voltage systems feature more sophisticated protection functions.

In high-voltage systems, vacuum circuit breakers are commonly used, such as in green solidification pots and oil circuit breakers. Medium-voltage switchgear typically features a drawer-type structure, equipped with both disconnect switches and fuses. The combination of fuses and disconnect switches functions similarly to a circuit breaker, though the latter offers greater operational convenience. Fuse-disconnect switch assemblies are primarily used to interrupt composite currents and leakage currents.

Low-voltage circuit breakers come in various types, including Molded Case Circuit Breakers (MCCB), usually installed in electrical distribution panels. Other variants include drawer-type, plug-in, and bolt-on models. GFCI breakers (Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter) are what we commonly refer to as leakage protection switches, while AFCI breakers (Arc Fault Circuit Interrupter) are specialized protective devices for residential use in North America. GFCIs primarily protect against ground faults, whereas AFCIs guard against arc faults.

There are also dedicated leakage protection switches for air conditioning systems. These all fall under the category of protective devices.

For example, fuses can be selected with either long-delay or short-delay characteristics based on different protection requirements. Disconnect switches are categorized into fusible and non-fusible types, as well as single-pole and double-pole configurations.

Contactors are primarily used in control circuits to interrupt load current rather than short-circuit current.  

Low-voltage circuit breakers involve two parameters: frame and tripping, typically labeled as 80oAF/AT. Here, 80oAF indicates the frame rating, while AT represents the tripping current setting, which can be configured as 600A or 500A, for example.  

Additionally, LSIG (Long-time, Short-time, Instantaneous, and Ground-fault) represents the four common protection functions of low-voltage circuit breakers. These are usually configured in the main incoming switch to provide overload, short-circuit, and ground-fault protection. Among them, the instantaneous protection function is specifically designed to rapidly interrupt short-circuit currents.

It features a Time-Current Curve, primarily used for calculating short-circuit current and its capacity, which requires evaluation based on the time-current curve.

Regarding circuit breakers, in North America, if the load is 800 amperes, a breaker rated at 800A can be selected when using a full rating; if the breaker is rated at 80%, a 1000A breaker must be chosen. When selecting a breaker, in addition to the load current, its interrupting capacity rating (IC rating) must also be considered. The minimum interrupting capacity for low-voltage breakers is 10kA, with other grades including 14kA, 22kA, 35kA, 42kA, and 65kA, where kA represents the breaker’s rated capacity to interrupt short-circuit current.

Regarding coordination, in a single-line system, coordination between upstream and downstream breakers is required. For example, a downstream breaker may only need a 22 kA interrupting capacity based on short-circuit current calculations, but the upstream breaker, being closer to the power source, may require a 35 kA breaker due to higher short-circuit current. If the distance between upstream and downstream breakers is short and the difference in short-circuit current is minimal, selecting a downstream breaker with a higher interrupting capacity may be cost-prohibitive. In such cases, a series rating solution can be adopted, where both upstream and downstream breakers trip simultaneously during a downstream short-circuit.

(Note: Technical terms such as “full rating,” “I_C rating,” and “series rating” are retained in English to preserve their technical context. Key parameter units like kA follow standard formatting.)

In terms of electrical equipment selection, it primarily involves medium-voltage switchgear, medium-voltage transformers, low-voltage switchgear, and low-voltage transformers. This discussion does not focus on specific selection methods but rather outlines the main electrical equipment to be considered during the design process. For example, in North America, common equipment includes step-down transformers (e.g., 600V or 480V to 208V), as well as generators, UPS, and ATS. Sometimes these are referred to as CDP (Central Distribution Panel) or MDP (Main Distribution Panel), which are essentially switchgear or standard distribution boards.

To improve power quality, power conditioners or power factor correction devices may be used, though their application is relatively limited. Other equipment includes MCC (Motor Control Centers) and VFD (Variable Frequency Drives). VFDs are primarily used for speed control and offer some protection and operational functions, though their protective capabilities are weak. MCCs are essentially integrated assemblies of motor starters.

Additional equipment includes metering devices like CT/PT and disconnect switches. Disconnect switches are mainly used for operational purposes and can only interrupt load current, not short-circuit current. The following section will introduce commonly used tools in the design process of power distribution systems.

In North America, there are three mainstream power system analysis software primarily used for medium and low-voltage systems. High-voltage systems utilize other software, which will not be discussed here. The main software in the distribution system field includes SKM, ETAP, and EasyPower, each developed by different companies.

Power system analysis and calculations are mainly categorized into the following types:

Loadflow Analysis: Used to calculate voltage drop, power factor, and load, which can generate panel schedules or assist in selecting electrical equipment specifications (Equipment Sizing).

Short Circuit Analysis.

Motor Starting Analysis.

Protective Coordination Study.

Short Circuit Analysis  
Motor Starting Analysis  
Protective Coordination Study  
Arc Flash Analysis: Quantifies the energy produced by distribution equipment during a short circuit, classifying each panel into one of four levels based on energy magnitude and labeling them accordingly. If the energy level is too high (Category 3 or 4), measures must be taken to reduce it below Category 2. Appropriate arc flash protective clothing is also required.  
Harmonics Analysis  
Generator Calculations: Applicable to scenarios with emergency power systems.  
In distribution system design, AutoCAD and Revit are primarily used for drafting.  
Regarding coordination with other disciplines, it is necessary to gather relevant information from other disciplines.

Domestically referred to as “design input provision”, we used to call it “submitting requirements”, which involves providing relevant information. For example, the heat generation situation in the power distribution room, the weight and dimensions of equipment, temperature and humidity requirements, fire protection requirements, as well as requirements for electrical equipment conduits, wall penetrations, foundations, etc.

Additionally, coordination issues with other disciplines need to be considered, such as who provides the VFD (Variable Frequency Drive) for motors, and who is responsible for wiring and commissioning—all of which must be clearly specified in the design documents.

For the air conditioning system, it is necessary to confirm whether control panels are equipped and if circuit breakers are already included. The air handling unit may include exhaust fans, return fans, and supply fans, and the power supply requirements for electric heaters must also be clarified.

The completeness of detailed technical specifications for all equipment, as well as the availability of existing data for the power distribution system, must be verified one by one.

Yes, I’ll skip the part about existing projects for now since it’s not very relevant to you. Also, we’re pressed for time today. Let me briefly explain the requirements for Fair Pump in the North American market.

NFPA 20 has distinct power supply requirements for fire pumps compared to other loads. Fire pumps are typically equipped with dedicated automatic transfer switches (ATS). When connected to both utility power and generators, fire pumps do not require overload protection, as they must operate continuously until equipment failure during fire emergencies. Additionally, the power supply for fire pumps must be directly connected to the utility power feed point, bypassing the main switchgear and connecting directly from the upstream switch.
